topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: London Dispersion Forces
topics.description: The weakest type of intermolecular force, present between all molecules and atoms, arising from temporary fluctuations in electron distribution.
learning_objectives: Explain the origin of London dispersion forces in terms of temporary dipoles
Explain why dispersion forces increase with molecular size/number of electrons
Apply this trend to predict and explain boiling point patterns
topics.explanation: London dispersion forces (also called van der Waals forces or induced dipole-induced dipole forces) are weak, temporary attractive forces that exist between all atoms and molecules, arising because electrons are in constant, random motion. At any given instant, electron distribution around an atom or molecule may become momentarily unequal, creating a temporary (instantaneous) dipole; this temporary dipole can induce a corresponding temporary dipole in a neighbouring atom or molecule, resulting in a brief, weak attraction between them. Because electron motion is constant and random, these temporary dipoles are constantly forming, disappearing, and re-forming in different orientations, but their overall net effect is a small, constant attractive force between particles. The strength of London dispersion forces increases with the number of electrons present (and therefore generally with increasing molecular size or relative molecular mass), since larger electron clouds are more easily distorted (more 'polarisable'), creating larger temporary dipoles and stronger induced attractions.
key_concepts: Temporary, fluctuating dipoles from electron motion
Induced dipole in a neighbouring particle
Present in ALL atoms/molecules
Strength increases with more electrons/larger molecular size

definitions.definition: A weak, temporary intermolecular attractive force arising from momentary, fluctuating uneven electron distribution, inducing a corresponding temporary dipole in a neighbouring particle.

worked_examples.problem: Explain why iodine (I2) is a solid at room temperature, while chlorine (Cl2) is a gas, given both are non-polar diatomic molecules held together only by London dispersion forces.
worked_examples.working: Iodine molecules have far more electrons than chlorine molecules (iodine atomic number 53 vs chlorine atomic number 17).
worked_examples.answer: Iodine's much larger number of electrons makes its electron cloud more easily distorted (more polarisable), creating stronger London dispersion forces between I2 molecules than between the smaller Cl2 molecules. These stronger dispersion forces in iodine require more energy to overcome, giving iodine a higher melting/boiling point, so it exists as a solid at room temperature while chlorine remains a gas.

practical_applications: Understanding dispersion forces explains the physical state trend down Group 17 (halogens) and the boiling point trend across a homologous series of alkanes, relevant to fuel and solvent selection in industry
laboratory_applications: Comparing measured boiling points across a homologous series (e.g. alkanes) as experimental evidence for the increase in dispersion force strength with increasing molecular size
common_mistakes: Assuming London dispersion forces are negligible or unimportant because they are the 'weakest' intermolecular force — in large molecules with many electrons, dispersion forces can actually become stronger overall than the dipole-dipole forces in a smaller polar molecule
misconceptions: Believing dispersion forces only exist in non-polar molecules — they exist between ALL atoms and molecules, including polar ones, in addition to any dipole-dipole forces or hydrogen bonding also present
tips: When comparing dispersion force strength between similar molecules, count or compare the number of electrons (or relative molecular mass, as a rough proxy) — more electrons generally means stronger dispersion forces

basic.question: State which type of intermolecular force is present between all atoms and molecules.
State what causes a temporary dipole to form in a molecule.
basic.answer: The random, constant motion of electrons, which can momentarily create an uneven distribution of electron density.

intermediate.question: Explain why the boiling point of alkanes increases as the length of the carbon chain increases (e.g. from methane to hexane).
intermediate.answer: As the carbon chain length increases, the number of electrons in the molecule increases, and the surface area available for contact between neighbouring molecules also increases. Both factors increase the strength of London dispersion forces between molecules, requiring more energy to overcome these forces during boiling, so boiling point increases with increasing chain length.

advanced.question: Explain why branched alkanes generally have lower boiling points than their straight-chain isomers with the same molecular formula (and therefore the same number of electrons).
advanced.answer: Although branched and straight-chain isomers have the same total number of electrons (and therefore similar overall polarisability), a branched molecule has a more compact, spherical shape with reduced surface area available for close contact with neighbouring molecules, compared to the more elongated shape of a straight-chain isomer, which can align closely along its length with neighbouring molecules. Since London dispersion forces depend on the closeness and surface area of contact between molecules (as well as the number of electrons), the reduced contact area in branched molecules results in weaker overall dispersion forces between molecules, giving branched isomers a lower boiling point than their straight-chain counterparts despite having an identical number of electrons.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why the boiling point of the noble gases increases going down Group 18, from helium to xenon, given that these are monatomic elements with no permanent dipole.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Noble gas atoms are held together in the liquid/solid state only by London dispersion forces, since they are non-polar and monatomic (no permanent dipole is possible) (1 mark). Moving down the group, atoms have progressively more electrons (helium has the fewest, xenon has many more) (1 mark). More electrons make the electron cloud more easily distorted (more polarisable), creating stronger temporary dipoles and stronger induced dispersion forces between atoms, so more energy is needed to separate them, giving increasing boiling points down the group (1 mark).

topics.summary: London dispersion forces are weak, temporary attractive forces present between all atoms and molecules, arising from fluctuating electron distribution inducing temporary dipoles. Their strength increases with the number of electrons (molecular size), explaining trends in melting/boiling points within related series of substances.
revision_notes: Present in ALL atoms/molecules (weakest force, but universal)
Origin: temporary/instantaneous dipole → induces dipole in neighbour
Strength increases with more electrons/larger molecular size/greater surface area contact

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Permanent Dipole Forces
topics.description: The attractive forces between polar molecules with a fixed, permanent uneven charge distribution, stronger than London dispersion forces alone.
learning_objectives: Explain the origin of permanent dipole-dipole forces
Distinguish permanent dipole forces from London dispersion forces
Compare the effect of permanent dipole forces vs dispersion forces on boiling point for similarly sized molecules
topics.explanation: Permanent dipole-dipole forces are attractive forces between polar molecules, arising from their fixed, permanent uneven distribution of charge (a permanent molecular dipole, resulting from polar bonds not cancelled out by symmetry — see Molecular Polarity). The positive (δ+) end of one polar molecule is attracted to the negative (δ−) end of a neighbouring polar molecule, and this attraction is generally stronger and more consistently oriented than the temporary, constantly fluctuating attraction from London dispersion forces alone. Permanent dipole forces act in addition to (not instead of) London dispersion forces, which are always present as well; polar molecules therefore generally have somewhat higher melting and boiling points than non-polar molecules of similar molecular size/number of electrons, due to this additional attractive force.
key_concepts: Attraction between permanent δ+ and δ− regions of neighbouring molecules
Acts in addition to dispersion forces (not instead of)
Generally stronger than dispersion forces alone for similar molecular size

definitions.definition: An attractive force between polar molecules, arising from the attraction between the permanent δ+ region of one molecule and the permanent δ− region of a neighbouring molecule.

worked_examples.problem: Explain why propanone (a polar molecule) has a higher boiling point than butane (a non-polar molecule of similar relative molecular mass).
worked_examples.working: Propanone contains a polar C=O bond, giving it a permanent molecular dipole; butane is non-polar, made only of non-polar C-C and near-non-polar C-H bonds.
worked_examples.answer: Propanone experiences both London dispersion forces and additional permanent dipole-dipole forces between its polar molecules, while butane experiences only the weaker London dispersion forces. This additional attractive force in propanone requires more energy to overcome, giving propanone a higher boiling point than butane, despite their similar relative molecular mass.

practical_applications: Permanent dipole forces influence the choice of polar solvents in chemical processes, since polar solvents interact favourably (via dipole-dipole forces) with other polar substances, aiding dissolution
laboratory_applications: Comparing boiling points of polar and non-polar molecules of similar relative molecular mass as evidence for the additional contribution of permanent dipole-dipole forces
common_mistakes: Forgetting that permanent dipole-dipole forces act in ADDITION to London dispersion forces, not as a replacement for them — a polar molecule experiences both types of force simultaneously
misconceptions: Believing permanent dipole-dipole forces are always stronger than dispersion forces in every comparison — for a very large non-polar molecule (many electrons) compared to a very small polar molecule (few electrons), the dispersion forces in the large non-polar molecule can actually be stronger overall
tips: When comparing boiling points of molecules with similar relative molecular mass, check for a permanent molecular dipole (polar bonds not cancelled by symmetry) — the polar molecule will generally have the higher boiling point, due to additional dipole-dipole attraction on top of dispersion forces

basic.question: State what causes permanent dipole-dipole forces to exist between molecules.
basic.answer: A permanent, uneven distribution of charge (a permanent molecular dipole) in polar molecules, due to polar bonds not cancelled out by molecular symmetry.

basic.question: State whether permanent dipole-dipole forces replace or add to London dispersion forces in a polar molecule.
basic.answer: They add to (act in addition to) London dispersion forces, which are always present as well.

intermediate.question: Explain why hydrogen chloride, HCl, has a higher boiling point than fluorine, F2, despite fluorine having a slightly greater relative molecular mass.
intermediate.answer: Hydrogen chloride is a polar molecule (due to the electronegativity difference between H and Cl), so it experiences both London dispersion forces and additional permanent dipole-dipole forces between molecules. Fluorine is a non-polar molecule (identical atoms, no permanent dipole), experiencing only London dispersion forces. The additional dipole-dipole attraction in HCl outweighs the very slightly weaker dispersion forces expected from its slightly lower relative molecular mass, giving HCl a higher boiling point than F2.

advanced.question: Explain why, despite propan-1-ol and butane having similar relative molecular masses, propan-1-ol has a considerably higher boiling point than the difference expected from permanent dipole-dipole forces alone would suggest.
advanced.answer: While propan-1-ol is indeed a polar molecule (due to its O-H bond) and experiences permanent dipole-dipole forces in addition to dispersion forces, unlike non-polar butane, the specific presence of an O-H bond allows propan-1-ol to form hydrogen bonds between its molecules — a particularly strong type of dipole-dipole interaction, considerably stronger than typical (non-hydrogen-bonding) permanent dipole-dipole forces. This additional hydrogen bonding, on top of ordinary dipole-dipole forces and dispersion forces, results in a boiling point considerably higher than would be expected from simple, non-hydrogen-bonding dipole-dipole forces alone, illustrating that the specific type and strength of intermolecular force present (not just whether a molecule is 'polar' in general) needs to be considered.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why propan-2-one (a polar molecule, Mr = 58) has a higher boiling point than butane (a non-polar molecule, Mr = 58), despite their identical relative molecular mass.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Both molecules experience London dispersion forces, which would be expected to be of similar strength given their identical relative molecular mass and similar number of electrons (1 mark). However, propan-2-one contains a polar C=O bond and has an overall permanent molecular dipole, allowing additional permanent dipole-dipole forces to act between its molecules, unlike the non-polar butane (1 mark). This additional attractive force in propan-2-one requires more energy to overcome, giving it a higher boiling point than butane despite their identical relative molecular mass (1 mark).

topics.summary: Permanent dipole-dipole forces arise between polar molecules with a fixed molecular dipole, acting in addition to London dispersion forces. They generally give polar molecules higher melting/boiling points than non-polar molecules of similar size, though very large non-polar molecules can still have stronger overall attractive forces due to dispersion alone.
revision_notes: Permanent dipole-dipole: attraction between fixed δ+/δ− regions of polar molecules
Acts IN ADDITION to (not instead of) dispersion forces
Generally: polar molecules have higher mp/bp than similarly sized non-polar molecules

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Hydrogen Bonding
topics.description: The strongest type of intermolecular force, occurring specifically between a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on a nearby N, O or F atom.
learning_objectives: State the specific structural requirements for hydrogen bonding to occur
Explain why hydrogen bonding is unusually strong compared to other dipole-dipole forces
Explain anomalous physical properties (e.g. water's high boiling point, ice floating) using hydrogen bonding
topics.explanation: Hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong type of intermolecular force that occurs specifically when a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded directly to one of the three highly electronegative, small atoms — nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine — and this hydrogen atom is then attracted to a lone pair of electrons on a nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine atom of a neighbouring molecule. This specific combination arises because N, O and F are small and highly electronegative, creating a very strong, concentrated partial positive charge on the hydrogen atom (since electron density is pulled strongly away from the small hydrogen nucleus), which is then strongly attracted to the concentrated negative charge of a nearby lone pair on another small, electronegative N, O or F atom. Hydrogen bonding, while still much weaker than a covalent bond, is considerably stronger than typical permanent dipole-dipole forces, and its presence explains several important anomalous properties, such as water's unusually high boiling point for its molecular size, and the fact that ice is less dense than liquid water (since hydrogen bonding holds water molecules in a relatively open, hexagonal lattice structure when frozen).
key_concepts: Requires H bonded to N, O or F
Requires a lone pair on a nearby N, O or F
Strongest intermolecular force (but weaker than covalent bonds)
Explains water's anomalous properties

definitions.definition: A particularly strong intermolecular force between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to N, O or F, and a lone pair of electrons on a nearby N, O or F atom.

worked_examples.problem: Explain why water has an unusually high boiling point compared to other similarly sized molecules such as methane, CH4.
worked_examples.working: Water contains O-H bonds, allowing hydrogen bonding between water molecules. Methane's C-H bonds do not permit hydrogen bonding, since carbon is not sufficiently electronegative and hydrogen is not bonded to N, O or F.
worked_examples.answer: Water's molecules are held together by relatively strong hydrogen bonds, in addition to weaker dispersion and dipole-dipole forces, requiring considerably more energy to separate during boiling. Methane only experiences weak London dispersion forces between its non-polar molecules, giving it a much lower boiling point despite water's smaller relative molecular mass.

practical_applications: Hydrogen bonding is fundamental to the structure of DNA (base pairing), proteins (secondary structure), and water's unique properties essential to life on Earth
laboratory_applications: Comparing the boiling points of a series of hydrides (e.g. NH3, H2O, HF vs their heavier group analogues) as experimental evidence for hydrogen bonding
common_mistakes: Believing hydrogen bonding can occur whenever hydrogen is present in a molecule — it specifically requires hydrogen to be bonded directly to N, O or F, and for the interaction to be with a lone pair on N, O or F in a neighbouring molecule; a C-H bond, for example, does not permit hydrogen bonding
misconceptions: Believing hydrogen bonds are as strong as covalent bonds — hydrogen bonds are considerably weaker than covalent bonds (roughly one-tenth the strength, though still the strongest of the intermolecular forces), which is why ice can still melt at a relatively low temperature despite extensive hydrogen bonding
tips: Use the mnemonic 'FON' (Fluorine, Oxygen, Nitrogen) to remember the only three elements involved in hydrogen bonding, both as the atom hydrogen is bonded to and as the atom providing the lone pair

basic.question: State the three elements that must be involved (directly bonded to hydrogen, and providing the lone pair) for hydrogen bonding to occur.
State whether hydrogen bonding is stronger or weaker than a covalent bond.
basic.answer: Weaker (though it is the strongest of the intermolecular forces).

intermediate.question: Explain why ammonia, NH3, can form hydrogen bonds, but phosphine, PH3, cannot, despite both containing hydrogen atoms bonded to a Group 15 element.
intermediate.answer: Nitrogen (in ammonia) is one of the three elements (N, O, F) that is sufficiently small and electronegative to create a strong enough partial positive charge on hydrogen and a sufficiently concentrated lone pair to permit hydrogen bonding. Phosphorus (in phosphine), despite being in the same group as nitrogen, has a much larger atomic radius and lower electronegativity, so it does not create a sufficiently strong dipole or sufficiently concentrated lone pair, meaning phosphine can only form weaker permanent dipole-dipole and dispersion forces, not hydrogen bonds.

advanced.question: Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water, referring to hydrogen bonding.
advanced.answer: In ice, water molecules are held in a fixed, open, hexagonal lattice arrangement by hydrogen bonds, with each water molecule hydrogen bonded to four neighbouring molecules in a specific tetrahedral arrangement that maximises hydrogen bonding but leaves relatively large, open gaps between molecules. In liquid water, molecules are more free to move and pack together somewhat more closely and randomly than in the rigid, open ice structure (though some hydrogen bonding is still present in the liquid), allowing water molecules on average to be packed slightly closer together in the liquid than in the more ordered, open lattice of ice. Because ice occupies a greater volume for the same mass of water compared to the liquid, ice has a lower density than liquid water, causing it to float.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why hydrogen fluoride, HF, has a much higher boiling point than hydrogen chloride, HCl, despite chlorine being a larger, heavier atom than fluorine.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Hydrogen fluoride can form hydrogen bonds between its molecules, since hydrogen is bonded directly to fluorine, one of the three elements (N, O, F) capable of hydrogen bonding, and fluorine has lone pairs available to accept a hydrogen bond from a neighbouring molecule (2 marks). Hydrogen chloride cannot form hydrogen bonds, since chlorine, despite being electronegative, is not one of the three specific elements (N, O, F) required, so HCl molecules are held together only by weaker permanent dipole-dipole forces and dispersion forces (1 mark). The considerably stronger hydrogen bonding in HF requires more energy to overcome than the weaker forces in HCl, giving HF the higher boiling point, despite HCl's larger relative molecular mass, which would otherwise be expected to increase dispersion forces (1 mark).

topics.summary: Hydrogen bonding is the strongest intermolecular force, occurring specifically when hydrogen is bonded to N, O or F and interacts with a lone pair on a neighbouring N, O or F atom. It explains anomalous properties such as water's high boiling point and ice's lower density than liquid water.
revision_notes: Hydrogen bonding requires: H bonded to N/O/F, AND a lone pair on nearby N/O/F
Strongest intermolecular force (but weaker than covalent bonds)
Mnemonic: FON
Explains: water's high bp, ice less dense than water, DNA base pairing
diagram_recommendations: [DIAGRAM: Hydrogen bonding between several water molecules, showing covalent O-H bonds and intermolecular hydrogen bonds]

images.description: Four simplified water molecules (each an oxygen atom with two attached hydrogen atoms) arranged with dashed lines connecting a hydrogen atom of one molecule to the oxygen (lone pair) of a neighbouring molecule, representing hydrogen bonds, with solid lines representing the covalent O-H bonds within each molecule, and a caption distinguishing the two line types.
images.purpose: Visually distinguishes the strong covalent O-H bonds within each water molecule from the weaker intermolecular hydrogen bonds between molecules, a distinction students frequently conflate.
images.placement: After the worked example, before the practice questions.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Molecular Polarity
topics.description: Whether a molecule has an overall permanent dipole, determined by both individual bond polarities and overall molecular shape/symmetry.
learning_objectives: Explain how molecular shape affects overall molecular polarity
Determine whether a molecule is polar or non-polar overall, given its bond polarities and shape
Explain why some molecules with polar bonds are non-polar overall
topics.explanation: The overall polarity of a molecule depends not only on whether it contains polar bonds, but also on the molecule's overall shape and symmetry, which determines whether the individual bond dipoles cancel out or combine to produce a net overall molecular dipole. If a molecule contains no polar bonds, it is always non-polar overall. If a molecule contains polar bonds arranged symmetrically (such that the individual bond dipoles point in directions that cancel out exactly, e.g. carbon dioxide's two identical, opposite C=O dipoles in a linear shape, or tetrachloromethane's four identical C-Cl dipoles in a symmetric tetrahedral shape), the molecule is non-polar overall, despite containing polar bonds. If a molecule contains polar bonds arranged asymmetrically (such that the bond dipoles do not fully cancel, e.g. water's bent shape, or a molecule with different substituents around a central atom), the molecule has an overall net dipole and is polar.
key_concepts: Polarity depends on bond polarity AND molecular shape/symmetry
Symmetric arrangement of identical polar bonds cancels dipoles (non-polar overall)
Asymmetric arrangement leaves a net dipole (polar overall)

definitions.definition: Whether a molecule has an overall permanent dipole, determined by the combination of its individual bond dipoles and its overall molecular shape.

worked_examples.problem: Explain why tetrachloromethane, CCl4, is non-polar overall, despite each individual C-Cl bond being polar.
worked_examples.working: CCl4 has a symmetric tetrahedral shape, with four identical C-Cl bonds arranged evenly (109.5° apart) around the central carbon atom.
worked_examples.answer: Because all four C-Cl bond dipoles are identical in magnitude and are arranged symmetrically around the central carbon, they cancel out exactly in all directions, resulting in no net overall molecular dipole, making CCl4 non-polar overall despite each individual bond being polar.

practical_applications: Molecular polarity determines solubility behaviour ('like dissolves like'), essential to choosing appropriate solvents in extraction, chromatography and industrial chemical processes
laboratory_applications: Testing the deflection of a thin stream of liquid by a charged rod as a simple experimental test for overall molecular polarity
common_mistakes: Assuming a molecule must be polar overall simply because it contains polar bonds, without checking whether the molecular shape allows those bond dipoles to cancel out by symmetry
misconceptions: Believing molecular shape alone determines polarity, without needing to consider bond polarity — a molecule with a symmetric shape but no polar bonds at all (e.g. methane, if C-H were considered fully non-polar) would also be non-polar, but for a different underlying reason; polarity requires considering both factors together
tips: Two-step check for overall molecular polarity: (1) are there any polar bonds present? If no, molecule is non-polar. (2) If yes, do the bond dipoles cancel out due to a symmetric arrangement? If they cancel, non-polar overall; if not, polar overall

basic.question: State two factors that determine whether a molecule is polar overall.
basic.answer: Whether it contains polar bonds, and the molecule's overall shape/symmetry (whether the bond dipoles cancel out).

basic.question: State whether carbon dioxide, CO2, is polar or non-polar overall.
basic.answer: Non-polar overall (its two C=O bond dipoles cancel due to its linear, symmetric shape).

intermediate.question: Explain why water, H2O, is polar overall, despite having a similar type of polar bond arrangement to carbon dioxide (two identical polar bonds to a central atom).
intermediate.answer: Unlike carbon dioxide, which has a linear shape with its two bond dipoles pointing in exactly opposite directions (cancelling out), water has a bent (non-linear) molecular shape, due to the two lone pairs of electrons on the central oxygen atom repelling the bonding pairs into a bent arrangement. Because the two O-H bond dipoles are not pointing in exactly opposite directions in this bent shape, they do not cancel out completely, resulting in a net overall molecular dipole pointing towards the oxygen atom, making water polar overall.

intermediate.question: Predict whether trichloromethane, CHCl3, is polar or non-polar overall, and explain your reasoning.
intermediate.answer: Trichloromethane is polar overall. Although it has a roughly tetrahedral shape similar to CCl4, it does not have full symmetry, since one of the four substituent atoms (hydrogen) is different from the other three (chlorine). Because the bond dipoles of the three C-Cl bonds and the one C-H bond are not all identical, they do not cancel out completely as they would in the fully symmetric CCl4, resulting in a net overall molecular dipole.

advanced.question: Explain why ammonia, NH3, is polar overall, using both bond polarity and molecular shape in your answer.
advanced.answer: Ammonia contains three N-H bonds, each of which is polar, since nitrogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, giving each bond a dipole pointing from hydrogen towards nitrogen. Ammonia has a trigonal pyramidal shape (due to one lone pair on nitrogen repelling the three bonding pairs into a pyramid rather than a flat triangle), which is not symmetric in the same way that a flat, trigonal planar or fully tetrahedral arrangement would be; specifically, the lone pair occupies a position at the 'top' of the pyramid with no equivalent bond dipole opposing it. As a result, the three N-H bond dipoles do not cancel out; they combine to produce a net overall molecular dipole pointing from the base of the pyramid towards the nitrogen atom (reinforced by the lone pair's own contribution to electron density in that direction), making ammonia polar overall.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why boron trifluoride, BF3, is non-polar overall despite containing three polar B-F bonds.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Each B-F bond is polar, since fluorine is more electronegative than boron (1 mark). However, BF3 has a symmetric trigonal planar shape, with the three identical B-F bonds arranged evenly at 120° to each other around the central boron atom (1 mark). Because the three identical bond dipoles are arranged symmetrically, they cancel out exactly, resulting in no net overall molecular dipole, making BF3 non-polar overall (1 mark).

topics.summary: Overall molecular polarity depends on both the presence of polar bonds and the molecule's shape/symmetry. Symmetric arrangements of identical polar bonds cause dipoles to cancel (non-polar overall, e.g. CO2, CCl4); asymmetric arrangements leave a net dipole (polar overall, e.g. H2O, NH3, CHCl3).
revision_notes: Check: (1) polar bonds present? (2) do dipoles cancel by symmetry?
Symmetric + identical polar bonds → non-polar overall (CO2, CCl4, BF3)
Asymmetric arrangement or lone pair present → polar overall (H2O, NH3, CHCl3)

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Bond Energy
topics.description: The energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state, used to estimate enthalpy changes of reaction.
learning_objectives: Define bond energy (bond enthalpy)
Use mean bond energies to estimate the enthalpy change of a reaction
Explain factors that affect the magnitude of bond energy
topics.explanation: Bond energy (or bond enthalpy) is the energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state, always an endothermic (positive) process. Because bond energy for a given type of bond (e.g. C-H) can vary slightly depending on the specific molecule it is found in, mean bond energies (averaged across many different molecules containing that bond) are typically used in calculations. Bond energies can be used to estimate the overall enthalpy change of a reaction by considering the energy required to break all the bonds in the reactants (endothermic, energy absorbed) and the energy released when all the new bonds in the products form (exothermic, energy released): enthalpy change ≈ (total energy to break bonds in reactants) − (total energy released forming bonds in products). Since this calculation uses mean, averaged bond energies (rather than the exact values for the specific molecules in that particular reaction), the result is only an estimate and may differ somewhat from the true, experimentally measured enthalpy change.
key_concepts: Bond energy: energy to break 1 mole of a bond, gaseous state, always endothermic
Mean bond energies used for estimation
Enthalpy change ≈ bonds broken (energy in) − bonds formed (energy out)

definitions.definition: The energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state; always a positive (endothermic) value.
An average value of bond energy for a particular type of bond, calculated across a range of different molecules containing that bond.

formulae.name: Enthalpy change estimation from bond energies
formulae.formula: ΔH ≈ Σ(bond energies broken) − Σ(bond energies formed)
formulae.description: Estimates the enthalpy change of a reaction using mean bond energy data for reactant and product bonds.

worked_examples.problem: Estimate the enthalpy change for the reaction H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g), given mean bond energies: H-H = +436 kJ/mol, Cl-Cl = +243 kJ/mol, H-Cl = +432 kJ/mol.
worked_examples.working: Bonds broken (reactants): 1 mol H-H + 1 mol Cl-Cl = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ/mol (energy absorbed). Bonds formed (products): 2 mol H-Cl = 2 × 432 = 864 kJ/mol (energy released). ΔH = 679 − 864.
worked_examples.answer: ΔH = −185 kJ/mol (exothermic, since more energy is released forming the new bonds than is absorbed breaking the original bonds)

practical_applications: Bond energy data is used to estimate the energy released or required in industrial reactions, fuel combustion, and to assess the thermal stability of compounds
laboratory_applications: Comparing bond-energy-estimated enthalpy changes to experimentally measured (calorimetry) values as a way of evaluating the reliability of mean bond energy data and identifying sources of discrepancy
common_mistakes: Forgetting that breaking bonds is always endothermic (energy absorbed, positive) and forming bonds is always exothermic (energy released, negative) — reversing this convention gives an incorrect sign for the final answer
Miscounting the number of each type of bond present in the reactants and products, especially in more complex molecules
misconceptions: Believing bond energy calculations give an exact, precise value for enthalpy change — since mean bond energies are averages across different molecules, the estimated value can differ from the true experimentally measured enthalpy change for the specific reaction in question, sometimes significantly
tips: Always write out clearly which bonds are broken (reactants) and which are formed (products), counting the exact number of each type present, before substituting into the equation ΔH ≈ bonds broken − bonds formed

basic.question: Define bond energy.
basic.answer: The energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state.

basic.question: State whether breaking a bond is exothermic or endothermic.

intermediate.question: Estimate the enthalpy change for the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g), given: N≡N = +945 kJ/mol, H-H = +436 kJ/mol, N-H = +391 kJ/mol.
intermediate.answer: Bonds broken: 1 × N≡N + 3 × H-H = 945 + (3×436) = 945 + 1308 = 2253 kJ/mol. Bonds formed: 2 × NH3, each with 3 N-H bonds = 6 × 391 = 2346 kJ/mol. ΔH = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ/mol.

intermediate.question: Explain why using mean bond energies gives only an estimate of enthalpy change, rather than an exact value.
intermediate.answer: Mean bond energies are average values calculated across many different molecules containing a particular type of bond, but the actual strength of a specific bond can vary slightly depending on the exact molecule and its surrounding structure/environment. Using an average value therefore introduces some uncertainty, meaning the calculated enthalpy change is only an estimate and may not exactly match the true, experimentally measured value for that specific reaction.

advanced.question: Explain why bond-energy-calculated enthalpy changes for reactions involving liquids or solids are generally less reliable than for reactions involving only gases.
advanced.answer: Bond energies are specifically defined for breaking bonds in the gaseous state, where molecules are widely separated and only the covalent bonds themselves need to be considered, with intermolecular forces being negligible. For reactions involving liquids or solids, additional energy changes occur due to intermolecular forces or lattice structures being broken or formed (e.g. converting a liquid reactant to a gas, or a gaseous product condensing to a liquid), which are not accounted for by bond energy values alone. This means bond-energy-based enthalpy calculations, which only consider covalent bond breaking/forming, become less accurate for reactions where states other than gases are involved, since they omit these additional intermolecular energy contributions.

exam_style_questions.question: Using mean bond energies (C-H = +413 kJ/mol, O=O = +498 kJ/mol, C=O = +805 kJ/mol, O-H = +463 kJ/mol), estimate the enthalpy change for the complete combustion of methane: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g).
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Bonds broken: 4 × C-H + 2 × O=O = (4×413) + (2×498) = 1652 + 996 = 2648 kJ/mol (1 mark). Bonds formed: 2 × C=O (in CO2) + 4 × O-H (in 2 H2O) = (2×805) + (4×463) = 1610 + 1852 = 3462 kJ/mol (1 mark). ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed = 2648 − 3462 = −814 kJ/mol (1 mark for correct method, 1 mark for correct final answer with correct sign).

topics.summary: Bond energy is the energy required to break one mole of a covalent bond in the gaseous state (always endothermic). Mean bond energies allow estimation of a reaction's enthalpy change (bonds broken − bonds formed), though this method only gives an approximate value.
revision_notes: Bond energy: always positive/endothermic (breaking bonds)
ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed)
Mean bond energies give only an ESTIMATE, not an exact value
Most reliable for gas-phase reactions only

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Bond Length
topics.description: The average distance between the nuclei of two covalently bonded atoms, and the factors affecting it.
learning_objectives: Define bond length
Explain how the number of shared electron pairs affects bond length
Explain how atomic radius of the bonded atoms affects bond length
topics.explanation: Bond length is the average distance between the nuclei of two atoms joined by a covalent bond, representing the equilibrium distance at which the attractive force (from shared electrons being attracted to both nuclei) balances the repulsive force (between the two positively charged nuclei, and between the electron clouds of both atoms). Bond length is affected by two main factors: the number of shared electron pairs (bond order), with more shared pairs resulting in greater electron density between the nuclei and therefore a shorter bond length (triple bonds are shorter than double bonds, which are shorter than single bonds, between the same two types of atom); and the atomic radii of the two bonded atoms, with larger atoms generally forming longer bonds, since their nuclei cannot approach as closely due to their larger overall electron cloud size.
key_concepts: Equilibrium distance between bonded nuclei
More shared pairs (higher bond order) → shorter bond
Larger atomic radii → longer bond

definitions.definition: The average equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two atoms joined by a covalent bond.

worked_examples.problem: Predict which bond is shorter: a C-C single bond or a C=C double bond, and explain why.
worked_examples.working: Compare the number of shared electron pairs: single bond = 1 pair; double bond = 2 pairs.
worked_examples.answer: The C=C double bond is shorter, since its greater number of shared electron pairs (2, compared to 1 in the single bond) creates greater electron density between the nuclei, resulting in stronger attraction and a shorter equilibrium distance between them.

practical_applications: Bond length data, determined experimentally (e.g. by X-ray crystallography or spectroscopy), is used to confirm molecular structures and bonding patterns in research and industrial quality control
common_mistakes: Forgetting to consider both factors (bond order AND atomic radius) when comparing bond lengths between different pairs of atoms — a bond between larger atoms with a higher bond order might not follow a simple, single-factor prediction
misconceptions: Believing bond length is a completely fixed, unchanging value for a given bond type in every possible molecule — while broadly similar, bond length can vary slightly depending on the specific molecule and its surrounding structure, similar to bond energy
tips: Remember two separate comparisons: (1) for bonds between the SAME two elements, more shared pairs = shorter bond (triple < double < single in length); (2) for single bonds between DIFFERENT pairs of elements, larger atomic radii = longer bond

basic.question: Define bond length.
basic.answer: The average equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two atoms joined by a covalent bond.

basic.question: State which is generally shorter: a single bond or a triple bond, between the same two atoms.

intermediate.question: Explain why the C-I bond is longer than the C-Cl bond.
intermediate.answer: Iodine has a considerably larger atomic radius than chlorine (since iodine is much further down Group 17). This means the iodine nucleus cannot approach as closely to the carbon nucleus as the smaller chlorine nucleus can, resulting in a greater equilibrium bond length for C-I compared to C-Cl.

advanced.question: Explain, in terms of both bond order and atomic radius, why comparing the length of a C=O double bond to a C-Cl single bond is not straightforward using either factor alone.
advanced.answer: Bond order suggests that a double bond (C=O, 2 shared pairs) should be shorter than a single bond (C-Cl, 1 shared pair) between the same or similar-sized atoms, since more shared electron pairs generally shorten a bond. However, atomic radius must also be considered: oxygen has a smaller atomic radius than chlorine, which would further shorten the C=O bond relative to a comparison based on atomic size alone, while chlorine's larger atomic radius would tend to lengthen the C-Cl bond. In this case, both factors (higher bond order and smaller atomic radius of oxygen) act in the same direction, both favouring a shorter C=O bond compared to C-Cl; however, in other comparisons, bond order and atomic radius effects could work in opposite directions, making a simple prediction using only one factor unreliable, and requiring both factors to be considered together (or experimental bond length data to be consulted) for an accurate comparison.

exam_style_questions.question: Explain why a C≡C triple bond is shorter than a C-C single bond, referring to electron density and nuclear attraction.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: A triple bond involves three shared pairs of electrons between the two carbon nuclei, compared to only one shared pair in a single bond (1 mark). This greater number of shared electron pairs results in greater electron density concentrated between the two nuclei (1 mark). This greater electron density creates a stronger overall attractive force pulling the two nuclei together, resulting in a shorter equilibrium bond length for the triple bond compared to the single bond (1 mark).

topics.summary: Bond length is the equilibrium distance between two covalently bonded nuclei, shortened by a greater number of shared electron pairs (higher bond order) and lengthened by larger atomic radii of the bonded atoms.
revision_notes: Bond length = equilibrium distance between bonded nuclei
More shared pairs (higher bond order) → shorter bond (same atoms)
Larger atomic radius (of bonded atoms) → longer bond

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Bond Strength
topics.description: The overall strength of a covalent bond, related inversely to bond length and directly to bond order, and its relationship to chemical reactivity.
learning_objectives: Explain the relationship between bond order, bond length and bond strength
Compare bond strength using bond energy data
Relate bond strength to chemical reactivity and stability
topics.explanation: Bond strength describes how strongly two atoms are held together by a covalent bond, most directly measured and compared using bond energy (the higher the bond energy, the stronger the bond). Bond strength is closely related to bond length and bond order: bonds with a higher bond order (more shared electron pairs, e.g. triple bonds) are generally both shorter and stronger than bonds with a lower bond order (e.g. single bonds) between the same two types of atom, since greater electron density between the nuclei both pulls them closer together and requires more energy to break apart. Bond strength has important chemical consequences: stronger bonds generally make a molecule more kinetically stable (less reactive, requiring more activation energy to break the bond during a reaction), as seen in the very strong triple bond of N2 making nitrogen gas relatively unreactive, while weaker bonds (such as the pi bond component of a double bond) tend to be more reactive and more readily broken during chemical reactions.
key_concepts: Bond strength measured by bond energy
Higher bond order → shorter AND stronger bond
Stronger bonds → generally less reactive/more kinetically stable

definitions.definition: A measure of how strongly two atoms are held together by a covalent bond, generally assessed using bond energy data.

worked_examples.problem: Using approximate bond energies (C-C = +347 kJ/mol, C=C = +612 kJ/mol), compare the strength of a single and double carbon-carbon bond.
worked_examples.working: Compare the bond energy values directly: higher bond energy indicates a stronger bond.
worked_examples.answer: The C=C double bond (612 kJ/mol) is considerably stronger than the C-C single bond (347 kJ/mol), consistent with its higher bond order (more shared electron pairs).

practical_applications: Bond strength data helps predict which bonds in a molecule are most likely to break first during a reaction, essential to understanding reaction mechanisms in organic and inorganic chemistry
common_mistakes: Assuming a double bond is exactly twice as strong as a single bond (or a triple bond exactly three times as strong) — while double and triple bonds are indeed stronger, the relationship is not a simple, exact multiplication, since the sigma and pi bond components contribute unequally to overall bond strength
misconceptions: Believing a stronger overall bond means every component of that bond is equally strong and unreactive — in a double bond, for example, the pi bond component is considerably weaker than the sigma bond component, making the pi bond more reactive even though the double bond as a whole is stronger than a single bond
tips: Link bond strength directly to reactivity in your explanations: strong bonds (e.g. N≡N) require high activation energy to break, contributing to low reactivity/kinetic stability, while comparatively weaker bonds (e.g. a pi bond) are more easily broken and more reactive

basic.question: State how bond strength is typically measured/compared.
basic.answer: Using bond energy — higher bond energy indicates a stronger bond.

basic.question: State whether a triple bond is generally stronger or weaker than a single bond between the same two atoms.

intermediate.question: Explain why the very strong triple bond in nitrogen gas, N2, makes it relatively unreactive at room temperature.
intermediate.answer: The triple bond in N2 has a very high bond energy, meaning a large amount of activation energy is required to begin breaking this bond during a reaction. This high activation energy makes reactions involving N2 proceed very slowly under normal conditions, giving nitrogen gas high kinetic stability and low reactivity, even though many reactions involving nitrogen are thermodynamically favourable overall.

advanced.question: Explain why alkenes are generally more reactive than alkanes, despite the C=C double bond in an alkene being stronger overall (higher bond energy) than the C-C single bond in an alkane.
advanced.answer: Although the C=C double bond as a whole has a higher total bond energy than a C-C single bond, this is because it is composed of two different components: a strong sigma bond (similar in strength to the single C-C sigma bond) plus a comparatively weaker pi bond. It is specifically this pi bond component that is more reactive, since its electron density (above and below the bond axis, from sideways p-orbital overlap) is less directly shielded between the nuclei and more accessible to attack by other reagents, allowing it to be broken relatively easily in addition reactions. Alkanes, containing only single (sigma) bonds, lack this exposed, reactive pi bond entirely, making them comparatively unreactive and requiring more forcing conditions (e.g. free-radical substitution) to react, despite their individual C-C bonds requiring less total energy to break than a C=C double bond.

exam_style_questions.question: Using bond energy data, explain why a C≡C triple bond is stronger than a C=C double bond, and explain one chemical consequence of this difference in strength.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: A triple bond has a higher bond energy than a double bond, since it involves three shared pairs of electrons (compared to two in a double bond), creating greater electron density and stronger overall attraction between the bonded nuclei (1 mark). This means more energy is required to break a triple bond than a double bond (1 mark). One consequence: alkynes, containing C≡C triple bonds, tend to have higher activation energies for reactions involving complete cleavage of the whole bond, though the exposed pi bond components of both double and triple bonds still make them reactive towards addition reactions (1 mark).

topics.summary: Bond strength, measured by bond energy, generally increases with bond order (more shared electron pairs) and correlates inversely with bond length. Stronger bonds contribute to kinetic stability and lower reactivity, though individual bond components (e.g. the pi bond within a double bond) can still be more reactive than the sigma bond component.
revision_notes: Bond strength ≈ bond energy; higher bond order = generally stronger (and shorter)
Strong bonds (e.g. N≡N) → high activation energy → kinetically stable/unreactive
Pi bond component of double/triple bonds is weaker/more reactive than sigma bond

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: VSEPR Theory
topics.description: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory, used to predict the three-dimensional shape of molecules based on minimising repulsion between electron pairs.
learning_objectives: State the basic principle of VSEPR theory
Explain why lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs
Use VSEPR theory to predict molecular shape from the number of bonding and lone pairs
topics.explanation: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory predicts the three-dimensional shape of a molecule based on the principle that pairs of electrons (both bonding pairs and lone pairs) around a central atom arrange themselves as far apart as possible in space, in order to minimise the repulsion between them. To predict a molecule's shape using VSEPR theory, the total number of electron pairs (bonding pairs plus lone pairs) around the central atom is first determined from its Lewis structure; these pairs then arrange themselves into a basic geometric shape that maximises the separation between them, before considering whether any of these positions are occupied by lone pairs rather than bonding pairs. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, because a lone pair is held closer to, and more concentrated around, the central atom's nucleus (being attracted to only one nucleus), while a bonding pair's electron density is spread out and shared between two nuclei; this difference in repulsion strength means the presence of lone pairs typically compresses the bond angles between the remaining bonding pairs slightly compared to the ideal, lone-pair-free geometric shape.
key_concepts: Electron pairs repel and arrange to minimise repulsion
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs
Order of repulsion strength: lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bonding pair > bonding pair-bonding pair

definitions.definition: A model that predicts molecular shape based on the principle that electron pairs (bonding and lone pairs) around a central atom arrange themselves to minimise mutual repulsion.

worked_examples.problem: Explain, using VSEPR theory, why the bond angle in ammonia (NH3, 107°) is smaller than the bond angle in methane (CH4, 109.5°).
worked_examples.working: Methane has 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around its central carbon atom. Ammonia has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around its central nitrogen atom.
worked_examples.answer: The lone pair in ammonia repels the three bonding pairs more strongly than a bonding pair would, compressing the H-N-H bond angle slightly below the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5° seen in methane (which has no lone pairs to cause this extra compression), giving ammonia its smaller observed bond angle of approximately 107°.

practical_applications: VSEPR theory is fundamental to predicting and explaining molecular shape and reactivity throughout organic and inorganic chemistry, essential to drug design and materials chemistry
common_mistakes: Forgetting to include lone pairs when counting the total number of electron pairs around a central atom — lone pairs affect the underlying electron pair geometry, even though they are not 'seen' in the final described molecular shape (e.g. 'bent' or 'trigonal pyramidal')
misconceptions: Believing molecular shape and electron pair geometry are always the same thing — electron pair geometry includes lone pairs in the arrangement, while molecular shape describes only the positions of the atoms (bonding pairs), which can differ (e.g. ammonia has a tetrahedral electron pair geometry but a trigonal pyramidal molecular shape)
tips: Always follow VSEPR predictions in two stages: (1) determine the total number of electron pairs and the resulting electron pair geometry (including lone pairs); (2) describe the molecular shape based on just the positions of the atoms, adjusting bond angles slightly if lone pairs are present

basic.question: State the basic principle of VSEPR theory.
basic.answer: Electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves as far apart as possible in space, to minimise repulsion between them.

basic.question: State whether lone pairs or bonding pairs cause greater repulsion.

intermediate.question: Explain why the bond angle in water (H2O, approximately 104.5°) is smaller than in ammonia (NH3, approximately 107°).
intermediate.answer: Water has two lone pairs on its central oxygen atom, while ammonia has only one lone pair on nitrogen. Since lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, and water has two lone pairs (causing two instances of this stronger repulsion effect on the bonding pairs) compared to ammonia's one lone pair, the bond angle in water is compressed even further below the ideal tetrahedral angle than in ammonia, giving water the smaller bond angle.

advanced.question: Explain the order of repulsion strength (lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bonding pair > bonding pair-bonding pair) in terms of electron density distribution.
advanced.answer: A lone pair of electrons is held and attracted by only a single nucleus (the central atom's nucleus), meaning its electron density is more concentrated and closer to that nucleus, occupying a comparatively larger, more spread-out region of space around the central atom. A bonding pair, in contrast, is shared between and attracted by two nuclei, which pulls its electron density into a more constrained, elongated region directly between the two bonded atoms, effectively making it 'thinner' and less repulsive at a given angular separation. Because lone pairs occupy more space and are held closer to the central atom, repulsion between two lone pairs is strongest; repulsion between a lone pair and a bonding pair is intermediate; and repulsion between two bonding pairs (both relatively confined between their respective pairs of nuclei) is weakest of the three combinations.

exam_style_questions.question: Using VSEPR theory, explain why methane (CH4) has bond angles of exactly 109.5°, while ammonia (NH3) has a slightly smaller bond angle.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Methane has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs around its central carbon atom; these four identical bonding pairs arrange themselves as far apart as possible, giving a perfectly symmetric tetrahedral shape with bond angles of exactly 109.5° (2 marks). Ammonia has three bonding pairs and one lone pair around its central nitrogen atom; the lone pair repels the three bonding pairs more strongly than a bonding pair would, compressing the H-N-H bond angle slightly below 109.5°, giving ammonia's smaller observed bond angle of approximately 107° (2 marks).

topics.summary: VSEPR theory predicts molecular shape based on electron pairs (bonding and lone pairs) arranging to minimise mutual repulsion. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, compressing bond angles below the ideal geometric value whenever lone pairs are present.
revision_notes: VSEPR: electron pairs arrange to minimise repulsion
Repulsion order: lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bonding pair > bonding pair-bonding pair
More lone pairs → smaller bond angles (compared to no-lone-pair ideal)

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Molecular Shapes
topics.description: The common three-dimensional shapes molecules adopt, as predicted by VSEPR theory, including linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal and bent shapes.
learning_objectives: Name and describe the common molecular shapes predicted by VSEPR theory
Predict molecular shape given the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs
Give an example molecule for each common shape
topics.explanation: Based on VSEPR theory, several common molecular shapes are frequently encountered. With 2 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs, a molecule is linear (180° bond angle, e.g. CO2, BeCl2). With 3 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs, a molecule is trigonal planar (120°, e.g. BF3). With 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs, a molecule is tetrahedral (109.5°, e.g. CH4). With 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair, a molecule is trigonal pyramidal (approximately 107°, e.g. NH3). With 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs, a molecule is bent/angular (approximately 104.5°, e.g. H2O). Each shape represents the arrangement that minimises repulsion between the electron pairs present, with lone pairs (where present) causing some compression of the bond angle compared to the equivalent shape with no lone pairs.
key_concepts: Linear (2 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs, 180°)
Trigonal planar (3, 0, 120°)
Tetrahedral (4, 0, 109.5°)
Trigonal pyramidal (3, 1, ~107°)

worked_examples.problem: Predict the shape of a molecule of boron trifluoride, BF3, given boron has 3 bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
worked_examples.working: 3 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs corresponds to the trigonal planar arrangement.
worked_examples.answer: BF3 is trigonal planar, with bond angles of 120°.

practical_applications: Molecular shape directly determines a molecule's physical properties (polarity, boiling point) and its biological activity (e.g. how a drug molecule fits into a receptor site), essential to pharmaceutical design
common_mistakes: Confusing trigonal pyramidal (NH3, with a lone pair, 3D shape) with trigonal planar (BF3, no lone pair, flat shape) — despite the similar names, these are different shapes with different bond angles
misconceptions: Believing a molecule's shape name always describes the arrangement of every electron pair (including lone pairs) — molecular shape names specifically describe the arrangement of atoms (bonding pairs) only, even though lone pairs influence that arrangement
tips: Build a mental reference table linking (bonding pairs, lone pairs) → shape name → approximate bond angle → example molecule, and practise applying it directly from a molecule's Lewis structure

basic.question: Name the shape of a molecule with 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs.
State the approximate bond angle in a trigonal planar molecule.

intermediate.question: Predict the shape and approximate bond angle of a water molecule, H2O, given oxygen has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs.
intermediate.answer: Water is bent (angular) in shape, with an approximate bond angle of 104.5°.

intermediate.question: Explain why carbon dioxide, CO2, is linear, given carbon has 2 bonding pairs (each a double bond) and no lone pairs.
intermediate.answer: With only 2 regions of electron density around the central carbon atom (counting each double bond as one region for shape purposes) and no lone pairs to cause additional repulsion or compression, the two bonding regions arrange themselves as far apart as possible, which is directly opposite each other at 180°, giving carbon dioxide its linear shape.

advanced.question: Explain why the sulfate ion, SO4^2−, is tetrahedral, even though sulfur can be considered to form double bonds to some of the oxygen atoms in one common representation of its structure.
advanced.answer: For VSEPR shape prediction purposes, each region of electron density around the central atom (whether it is a single bond, a double bond, or a lone pair) is generally counted as one repelling region, regardless of whether that region contains one or more shared pairs of electrons. In the sulfate ion, sulfur is surrounded by four oxygen atoms (via four separate regions of bonding electron density, whether represented with some double bonds or, in a more detailed picture, delocalised bonding), with no lone pairs on sulfur. These four regions of electron density arrange themselves as far apart as possible, giving the characteristic tetrahedral shape with bond angles of approximately 109.5°, regardless of the finer details of exactly how the bonding electrons are distributed within each region.

exam_style_questions.question: State the shape and approximate bond angle of ammonia, NH3, and explain how this shape arises from VSEPR theory.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: Ammonia has a trigonal pyramidal shape, with an approximate bond angle of 107° (1 mark). Nitrogen has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair; these four regions of electron density arrange themselves to minimise repulsion, adopting an underlying tetrahedral electron pair geometry (1 mark). Since the lone pair repels the bonding pairs more strongly than a bonding pair would, and is not itself counted as part of the visible molecular shape (which describes only atom positions), the observed shape is trigonal pyramidal, with the bond angle compressed slightly below the ideal tetrahedral 109.5° (1 mark).

topics.summary: Common molecular shapes predicted by VSEPR theory include linear (180°), trigonal planar (120°), tetrahedral (109.5°), trigonal pyramidal (~107°), and bent (~104.5°), determined by the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom.
revision_notes: Linear: 2 bp, 0 lp, 180° (CO2)
Trigonal planar: 3 bp, 0 lp, 120° (BF3)
Tetrahedral: 4 bp, 0 lp, 109.5° (CH4)
Trigonal pyramidal: 3 bp, 1 lp, ~107° (NH3)
Bent: 2 bp, 2 lp, ~104.5° (H2O)
diagram_recommendations: [DIAGRAM: Five common molecular shapes (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, bent) with example molecules and bond angles]

images.description: Five small ball-and-stick style diagrams arranged side by side, showing linear (CO2, 180 deg), trigonal planar (BF3, 120 deg), tetrahedral (CH4, 109.5 deg), trigonal pyramidal (NH3, 107 deg, with lone pair indicated), and bent (H2O, 104.5 deg) shapes, each labelled with its name, example formula, and bond angle.
images.purpose: Gives students a single consolidated visual reference for all five common VSEPR-predicted shapes, allowing direct side-by-side comparison of geometry and bond angle across the full progression.
images.placement: After the worked example, before the practice questions.

topics.subject: Chemistry
topics.title: Bond Angles
topics.description: The angle between two bonds sharing a common atom, determined by VSEPR theory and the number/type of surrounding electron pairs.
learning_objectives: Define bond angle
State the standard bond angles associated with each common molecular shape
Explain deviations from ideal bond angles due to lone pairs or differing substituents
topics.explanation: A bond angle is the angle formed between two covalent bonds that share a common atom, measured in degrees. Bond angles are predicted using VSEPR theory, based on the number and type of electron pairs (bonding and lone) around the central atom: 180° for a linear arrangement (2 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs), 120° for trigonal planar (3 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs), 109.5° for tetrahedral (4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs), approximately 107° for trigonal pyramidal (3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair), and approximately 104.5° for bent/angular (2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs). Each additional lone pair present typically reduces the bond angle slightly compared to the equivalent all-bonding-pair shape, due to the stronger repulsion exerted by lone pairs. Bond angles can also be affected by differences between the substituent atoms bonded to the central atom, or by differing electronegativity, which can cause small deviations from these idealised, textbook values in real molecules.
key_concepts: Standard bond angles for each shape (180°, 120°, 109.5°, ~107°, ~104.5°)
Lone pairs reduce bond angle compared to all-bonding-pair equivalent
Real molecules can deviate slightly from idealised angles

definitions.definition: The angle, measured in degrees, between two covalent bonds that share a common central atom.

worked_examples.problem: State the approximate H-N-H bond angle in ammonia, and explain why it is not exactly 109.5°.
worked_examples.working: Ammonia has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair, an underlying tetrahedral electron pair geometry (ideal angle 109.5°), but the lone pair causes additional compression.
worked_examples.answer: The H-N-H bond angle in ammonia is approximately 107°, slightly less than the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5°, because the lone pair on nitrogen repels the three bonding pairs more strongly than a bonding pair would, compressing the angle between them.

practical_applications: Precise bond angle measurements (from spectroscopic and diffraction techniques) are used to confirm predicted molecular structures in chemical research and drug design
common_mistakes: Assuming every molecule with 4 electron pairs around its central atom has an identical bond angle of exactly 109.5° — this ideal value applies only when all 4 pairs are bonding pairs (no lone pairs); the presence of lone pairs reduces the angle
misconceptions: Believing bond angles are always exactly the textbook 'ideal' values in every real molecule — actual measured bond angles can deviate slightly from these idealised values due to factors such as differing substituent electronegativities or steric effects, even within molecules sharing the same basic VSEPR-predicted shape
tips: Memorise the five key bond angle values (180°, 120°, 109.5°, ~107°, ~104.5°) alongside their corresponding shape names and a representative example molecule for each

basic.question: Define bond angle.
basic.answer: The angle, measured in degrees, between two covalent bonds that share a common central atom.

basic.question: State the ideal bond angle in a tetrahedral molecule.

intermediate.question: State the bond angles in carbon dioxide, boron trifluoride and methane, and explain the general trend in these values.
intermediate.answer: CO2 (linear): 180°; BF3 (trigonal planar): 120°; CH4 (tetrahedral): 109.5°. As the number of bonding pairs around the central atom increases (with no lone pairs present in any of these examples), the electron pairs must arrange themselves closer together to remain as far apart as possible in three-dimensional space (or two dimensions, for the flat trigonal planar shape), resulting in progressively smaller bond angles as more bonding pairs are added.

advanced.question: Explain why the F-N-F bond angle in nitrogen trifluoride, NF3 (a trigonal pyramidal molecule like NH3), is very close to 102°, slightly smaller than the H-N-H angle in ammonia (~107°), despite both having the same basic shape (3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair on nitrogen).
advanced.answer: Both molecules have the same underlying VSEPR shape (trigonal pyramidal, 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair on nitrogen), so the general compression effect from the lone pair applies to both. However, fluorine is considerably more electronegative than hydrogen, so in NF3 the bonding electron pairs are pulled more strongly away from nitrogen and towards each fluorine atom, compared to the N-H bonding pairs in ammonia, which remain more evenly distributed/closer to nitrogen (since hydrogen is less electronegative than nitrogen). This means the N-F bonding pairs are, on average, positioned slightly further from the nitrogen's lone pair (which stays localised on nitrogen) than the N-H bonding pairs are, altering the balance of repulsions in a way that results in a smaller observed bond angle for NF3 (~102°) compared to NH3 (~107°), illustrating that electronegativity differences between substituents can cause bond angles to deviate from a simple prediction based on lone pair count alone.

exam_style_questions.question: State the bond angle in a molecule of water, and explain why it is smaller than the bond angle in ammonia.
exam_style_questions.model_answer: The bond angle in water is approximately 104.5° (1 mark). Water has two lone pairs on its central oxygen atom, compared to ammonia's single lone pair on nitrogen (1 mark). Since lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, and water has two lone pairs causing this stronger repulsion (compared to ammonia's one), the bond angle in water is compressed further below the ideal tetrahedral angle than in ammonia, giving water the smaller bond angle of the two (1 mark).

topics.summary: Bond angles, predicted by VSEPR theory, follow standard values for each molecular shape (180°, 120°, 109.5°, ~107°, ~104.5°), reduced from the ideal all-bonding-pair value whenever lone pairs are present, and can deviate slightly further due to differences in substituent electronegativity.
revision_notes: Standard bond angles: 180° (linear), 120° (trig. planar), 109.5° (tetrahedral), ~107° (trig. pyramidal), ~104.5° (bent)
More lone pairs → smaller bond angle
Electronegativity differences between substituents can cause further small deviations
